113030.e: Dill and fennel both have hair-fine, divided leaves and are closely related members of the carrot family. You can easily tell them apart by their taste.
113030.m: Fennel leaves look very similar to dill.

113031.q: Which butterfly likes to lay its eggs on fennel, dill and carrot?
113031.e: Swallowtail caterpillars feed on members of the carrot family such as fennel, dill, carrot and wild carrot. In the garden you sometimes find the green, black and orange striped caterpillars right on the fennel.
113031.m: The swallowtail caterpillar likes eating fennel.

113032.q: Which part of Florence fennel is eaten as a vegetable?
a: The thickened leaf bases that form a bulb
113032.e: In Florence fennel, the thick leaf stalks wrap around each other at the bottom to form a bulb. This is eaten raw in salad or cooked.
113032.m: With Florence fennel, you eat the bulb made of thickened leaf bases.

113033.q: Botanically speaking, what are so-called fennel seeds?
113033.e: What you buy as fennel seeds are really small split fruits. Each one contains a seed.
113033.m: Botanically, fennel seeds are small fruits.

113034.q: Which region does fennel originally come from?
113034.e: Wild fennel grows on the coasts of the Mediterranean. The Romans and Greeks already used it as a spice and medicinal plant.

113035.q: What do fennel leaves look like?
113035.e: Fennel leaves are divided into many hair-fine tips. They are also used as a kitchen herb.
113035.m: Fennel leaves are fine and thread-like.

113036.q: What does the underside of silverweed leaves look like?
113036.e: The feathery leaves are thickly covered with silvery hairs underneath. That is why the plant is called silverweed.
113036.m: Silverweed has silvery undersides to its leaves.

113037.q: Where does the first part of the German name of silverweed, “Gänsefingerkraut” (goose finger herb), come from?
a: It likes to grow on goose pastures
It only grows on geese's necks
113037.e: The plant is common on pastures and by village ponds, where geese used to be kept. Geese like eating it.
113037.m: Silverweed likes to grow where geese graze.

113038.e: Silverweed has single yellow flowers with five petals. They sit on long stalks.

113039.q: Which plant family does silverweed belong to?
113039.e: Silverweed is closely related to the cinquefoils. Like the rose, apple and strawberry, these belong to the rose family.
113039.m: Silverweed belongs to the rose family.

113040.q: How does silverweed spread across the ground?
a: With seeds that fly like parachutes
It does not, it stays on its own
113040.e: Silverweed forms runners above ground that put down roots. This creates whole carpets of plants, similar to strawberries.

113041.q: What is silverweed traditionally used against?
113041.e: In folk medicine, silverweed is said to relieve cramps. People drink it as a tea for stomach cramps.
113041.m: Silverweed is traditionally used against stomach cramps.

113042.q: Which substances make silverweed tea helpful for mild diarrhoea?
113042.e: Tannins slightly tighten the mucous membranes. This can help with mild diarrhoea.
113042.m: Tannins in silverweed help with mild diarrhoea.

113043.e: Each leaf is made of many small, toothed leaflets. They sit in pairs on a shared stalk.

113044.q: What does willow bark tea taste like?
113044.e: Willow bark contains tannins and bitter substances. So the tea tastes bitter and makes your mouth pucker a little.
113044.m: Willow bark tea tastes bitter and harsh.

113045.q: Where does the name of the active substance salicin come from?
a: From the Latin name of the willow, Salix
113045.e: Willows form the genus Salix. The names salicin and salicylic acid come from this.
113045.m: Salicin is named after the willow, Salix in Latin.

113046.q: Who should not take willow bark because of an intolerance?
113046.e: Willow bark contains substances called salicylates, similar to those in the painkiller aspirin. People who are oversensitive to these should avoid it.
113046.m: If you cannot tolerate aspirin, do not take willow bark either.

113047.q: Which well-known painkiller was developed by copying the active substances in willow bark?
113047.e: Acetylsalicylic acid was later developed from the willow substance salicin. It went on sale as aspirin at the end of the 19th century.
113047.m: Aspirin was developed by copying willow bark.

113048.q: Which complaints is willow bark often used for in herbal medicine today?
a: For mild back and joint pain
113048.e: Herbal medicines with willow bark are used mainly for mild back pain and rheumatic complaints. They are weaker than modern painkillers.
113048.m: Today willow bark is often used for mild back and joint pain.

113049.q: According to the European Medicines Agency, who are medicines made from willow bark not recommended for?
113049.e: As with aspirin, there is not enough safety data for children and teenagers. That is why the European Medicines Agency advises against it for under-18s.
113049.m: Willow bark is not recommended for children and teenagers.

113050.q: Why does willow bark tea work more slowly than an aspirin tablet?
a: The body first has to convert the salicin
Tea is not absorbed by the body
Willow bark contains no active substance at all
Hot water destroys all active substances at once
113050.e: Salicin is a precursor. Only in the gut and liver is it turned into the active salicylic acid, and that takes time.
113050.m: The salicin from willow bark first has to be converted in the body.

113051.q: Which part of the willow is used for the remedy?
113051.e: The bark is peeled from young twigs, two to three years old, in spring. That is where the content of the active substance is high.
113051.m: Willow bark tea is made from the bark of young twigs.

113052.q: The name aspirin contains the syllable “spir”. Which plant does it come from?
113052.e: Salicylic acid used to be obtained from meadowsweet, which was then called Spiraea. The “A” stands for acetyl and “spir” for Spiraea.
113052.m: The name aspirin contains Spiraea, the old name for meadowsweet.

113053.q: Which organ do the active substances in foxglove affect?
113053.e: The active substances in foxglove make the heart muscle beat more strongly. But in too large an amount they are deadly.
113053.m: Foxglove contains substances that act on the heart.

113054.q: What do the flowers of the common foxglove look like?
a: Like bells on a tall flower spike
Like flat stars on the ground
113054.e: The common foxglove forms a tall flower spike with many hanging, tube-shaped bells. Inside they are often spotted with dark marks.
113054.m: The common foxglove has bell-shaped flowers on a tall stem.

113057.q: Where does the common foxglove especially like to grow in nature?
a: In forest clearings with acid soil
In salt water on the beach
On glaciers in the eternal ice
113057.e: The common foxglove likes bright spots in the forest, such as clearings and areas where trees have been felled. It prefers acid soils low in lime.
113057.m: The common foxglove likes to grow in forest clearings.

113058.q: Which harmless plant are foxglove leaves sometimes dangerously confused with before the plant flowers?
113058.e: Before it flowers, foxglove forms only a rosette of hairy leaves. These look like comfrey leaves, which has already led to poisonings.
113058.m: Foxglove leaves can be confused with comfrey.

113059.q: What colour are the flowers of the large yellow foxglove and the small yellow foxglove, which grow wild in Switzerland?
113059.e: The large yellow foxglove and the small yellow foxglove have pale yellow flowers and grow in Swiss forests and at forest edges. Like the common foxglove, they are poisonous.
113059.m: Yellow-flowered kinds of foxglove grow wild in Switzerland.

113060.q: Why must people never make foxglove into tea themselves?
a: The healing amount and the poisonous amount are very close together
It does not dissolve in water
113060.e: With foxglove's active substances, the gap between an effective dose and a poisonous dose is very small. That is why they are only prescribed as medicines in exact doses.
113060.m: With foxglove, the difference between medicine and poison is very small.

113061.e: Sebastian Kneipp was a Catholic priest. As the priest of a Bavarian village, he treated many people with water treatments.
113061.m: Sebastian Kneipp was a Catholic priest.

113062.q: Which element is the Kneipp cure especially linked with?
113062.e: Kneipp relied on showers, wraps and baths with cold water. They are meant to strengthen the circulation and the body's defences.
113062.m: The Kneipp cure relies mainly on cold water.

113063.q: According to Sebastian Kneipp, what else besides water is part of a healthy life?
a: As much time in bed as possible
113063.e: Kneipp's teaching rests on five pillars: water, medicinal plants, exercise, diet and a balanced way of life. Together they are meant to strengthen the whole person.
113063.m: Kneipp's teaching also includes exercise and healthy food.

113064.q: Which treatment is typical of Kneipp facilities, which also exist in Switzerland?
a: Wading through water with a stork walk
113064.e: You walk through cold water about as deep as your calves, lifting your legs high like a stork. This is meant to boost blood flow.
113064.m: When water wading, you walk like a stork through cold water.

113065.q: In which century did Sebastian Kneipp live?
113065.e: Sebastian Kneipp lived from 1821 to 1897. His teaching became world-famous towards the end of the 19th century.
113065.m: Sebastian Kneipp lived in the 19th century.

113066.q: What made Sebastian Kneipp famous far beyond his village?
a: A book about his water cure
113066.e: In 1886 Kneipp's book “My Water Cure” was published. It was translated into many languages and made him world-famous.
113066.m: Kneipp became famous with his book about the water cure.

113067.q: According to his own account, how did the young Sebastian Kneipp cure himself of his serious lung disease?
a: With short baths in the cold Danube
With long trips to the seaside
113067.e: Kneipp fell ill with tuberculosis as a student. He bathed several times briefly in the ice-cold water of the Danube and believed this was why he got better.
113067.m: As a young man, Kneipp bathed in the cold Danube to get well.

113068.q: What do you do in a Kneipp spa town?
a: You recover with water treatments and exercise
113068.e: In Kneipp spa towns such as Bad Wörishofen, where Kneipp himself worked, there are wading pools, water showers and walking paths. Guests are meant to build up new strength.
113068.m: In Kneipp spa towns you recover with water and exercise.

113069.q: On which river is Bingen, which Hildegard is named after?
113069.e: Bingen lies on the Rhine in Germany, where the Nahe flows into the Rhine. Hildegard founded her convent nearby.

113070.q: Which cereal did Hildegard of Bingen value especially highly?
113070.e: Hildegard praised spelt as especially easy to digest. That is why spelt is still often linked with her today.
113070.m: Hildegard of Bingen especially valued spelt.

113071.q: Apart from religion, what did Hildegard of Bingen also write books about?
113071.e: In works such as the “Physica”, she described plants, animals and stones and how they are useful for health. Her writings are seen as early sources of natural history.
113071.m: Hildegard of Bingen wrote about nature and medicine.

113072.q: Which art was Hildegard of Bingen also active in?
a: She painted oil paintings on canvas
113072.e: Hildegard wrote many religious songs. Her music is still performed and recorded today.
113072.m: Hildegard of Bingen composed religious music.

a: A nun and abbess of a convent
113073.e: Hildegard lived in the 12th century and led a convent on the Rhine as its abbess. She wrote about faith, nature and medicine and composed music.
113073.m: Hildegard of Bingen was a nun and abbess.

113074.q: What did Hildegard of Bingen call the life force that makes all living things grow?
113074.e: Hildegard spoke of “viriditas”, the greening power. By this she meant the force of life and growth in plants, animals and people.
113074.m: Hildegard called nature's life force the greening power.

113075.q: What did Hildegard of Bingen write about in her work “Scivias”?
113075.e: Hildegard said she had had visions since childhood. In “Scivias”, which means “Know the Ways”, she wrote them down.

113076.q: In which present-day Swiss canton was Paracelsus born?
113076.e: Paracelsus was born around 1493 in Egg near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz. His father was a doctor there.
113076.m: Paracelsus was born near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz.

113077.q: Which science did Paracelsus want to use more in medicine by making remedies from minerals and metals?
113077.e: Paracelsus made remedies from substances such as mercury, sulphur or antimony. That is why he is seen as a pioneer of pharmaceutical chemistry.

113078.e: Paracelsus was a doctor, natural scientist and philosopher. He travelled all over Europe and worked, among other things, as the town doctor in Basel.
113078.m: Paracelsus was a doctor and natural scientist.

113079.q: In which language did Paracelsus unusually give his lectures in Basel?
113079.e: At that time scholars taught almost only in Latin. In Basel, Paracelsus spoke German so that more people could understand him.
113079.m: Paracelsus gave his lectures in German.

113080.q: What did Paracelsus want to express with his name?
a: That he surpassed the Roman doctor Celsus
That he was a pupil of Celsus
That he was born in Paracel
113080.e: “Para” means roughly “beyond”. The name is often taken to mean that he wanted to go beyond the famous Roman doctor Celsus.
113080.m: The name Paracelsus refers to the Roman doctor Celsus.

113081.q: What did Paracelsus publicly burn in Basel in 1527 to protest against the old medicine?
113081.e: Paracelsus threw a work by the doctor Avicenna into the Midsummer bonfire. He wanted to show that you should not just believe old books but observe for yourself.
113081.m: Paracelsus burnt an old medical book in Basel in protest.

113082.q: What does the doctrine of signatures, which Paracelsus supported, say?
a: The look of a plant shows what it heals
Plants should be labelled with names
Plants only work at full moon
113082.e: According to this old teaching, for example, a heart-shaped plant helps the heart. Science has not confirmed this idea.
113082.m: According to the doctrine of signatures, a plant's look shows its healing power.

113083.e: The Greek word “phyton” means plant. So phytotherapy is herbal medicine.

113084.q: In pharmacy, what is a dried plant part used as a remedy called?
113084.e: In pharmacy, a dried plant part such as camomile flowers or valerian root is called a crude drug. Here this has nothing to do with illegal drugs.
113084.m: In pharmacy, dried parts of medicinal plants are called crude drugs.

113085.q: What do you call a tea where you pour hot water over the herbs and leave them to steep?
113085.e: For an infusion, you pour boiling water over delicate plant parts such as flowers and leaves. Hard parts such as roots, on the other hand, are often boiled.
113085.m: For an infusion, you pour hot water over herbs.

113086.q: What is a plant extract made with alcohol called?
113086.e: For a tincture, plant parts are soaked in alcohol. This draws out the active substances and makes the extract keep for a long time.
113086.m: A tincture is a plant extract made with alcohol.

113087.q: Which substances give peppermint, camomile and fennel their strong scent?
113087.e: Essential oils evaporate easily and smell strong. Many of them relieve cramps or reduce inflammation.
113087.m: Essential oils give many medicinal plants their scent.

113088.q: Why should you only gather medicinal plants in nature if you can recognise them for certain?
a: Because you can confuse them with poisonous plants
Because all medicinal plants are banned
Because otherwise they wilt at once
Because they only work at night
113088.e: Some medicinal plants look very much like poisonous species. Confusing them can be dangerous.
113088.m: Only gather medicinal plants if you can recognise them for certain.

113089.q: What are healing methods such as herbal medicine, which add to conventional medicine, called?
113089.e: Complementary means adding to something. Phytotherapy is part of complementary medicine, which has been in the Federal Constitution since 2009.
113089.m: Phytotherapy is part of complementary medicine.

113090.q: Which tea made from a medicinal plant is often drunk for tummy ache?
113090.e: Camomile flowers have a calming and anti-inflammatory effect. Camomile tea is one of the best-known home remedies from herbal medicine.
113090.m: Camomile tea is a well-known home remedy for tummy ache.

113091.q: Which authority approves medicines in Switzerland, including those made from plants?
113091.e: Swissmedic is the Swiss authority that approves and supervises medicines. Herbal medicines also need approval.

113092.q: What typically happens to the resting pulse when someone does regular endurance training for months?
113092.e: A trained heart pumps more blood with each beat. So at rest it needs to beat less often.
113092.m: Regular endurance training lowers the resting pulse.

113093.q: What is the type of training called in which short, intense efforts alternate with recovery breaks?
113093.e: In interval training, hard sections are followed by planned breaks. This lets you run or ride very intensely several times.
113093.m: In interval training, effort and rest alternate.

113094.q: How long does the classic Cooper test last, in which you run as far as possible?
113094.e: The doctor Kenneth Cooper developed the test: you run as far as possible for 12 minutes. The distance shows your endurance.
113094.m: In the Cooper test, you run as far as possible in 12 minutes.

113095.q: What is the type of training called in which you run for a long time without a break at a steady, calm pace?
113095.e: With the continuous method, you keep moving for, say, 30 to 60 minutes without stopping. It mainly improves basic endurance.
113095.m: With the continuous method, you train for a long time without a break.

113096.q: During easy endurance training, what is a good sign that the pace is not too high?
113096.e: At a calm pace, your breath is still enough for whole sentences. This rule of thumb is often called “running without puffing”.
113096.m: If you can still chat during easy training, you are running at the right pace.

113097.q: Which of these sports mainly trains endurance?
113097.e: In cross-country skiing you move for a long time at a steady pace. Weightlifting, shot put and high jump are short bursts of strength.
113097.m: Cross-country skiing is a typical endurance sport.

113098.q: What is an enlarged, efficient heart resulting from endurance training called?
113098.e: With lots of endurance training, the heart muscle becomes bigger and stronger. In healthy athletes, this is a normal adaptation to training.
113098.m: A heart strengthened by training is called an athlete’s heart.

113099.q: Apart from the muscles, which body system is particularly strengthened by endurance training?
113099.e: Endurance needs a lot of oxygen in the muscles. That is why the heart, blood vessels and lungs in particular adapt.
113099.m: Endurance training strengthens the heart and circulation.

113100.q: What is the ability to repeat a force as often or as long as possible without getting tired called?
113100.e: You need strength endurance for rowing or doing lots of press-ups, for example. The muscles must produce force over a longer time.
113100.m: Strength endurance means being able to use strength for a long time.

113101.q: Which type of strength does a sprinter particularly need at the start to push off explosively?
113101.e: Explosive strength is the ability to develop a lot of force in a very short time. It is important for sprints and jumps.
113101.m: For explosive movements, you need explosive strength.

113102.q: What is the greatest force a muscle can produce in a single effort called?
113102.e: Maximum strength shows, for example, in the heaviest weight you can lift exactly once.
113102.m: Maximum strength is the highest possible force of a muscle.

113103.q: What is a group of several repetitions of a strength exercise, followed by a break, called?
113103.e: In strength training you might do 3 sets of 12 repetitions each. Between the sets, the muscle recovers briefly.
113103.m: Several repetitions in a row make up a set.

113104.q: What is an exercise called in which you hold your body still in one position, as in the plank?
113104.e: In a holding exercise, the muscles tense without the joints moving. The plank and the wall sit are typical examples.
113104.m: In the plank, the muscles hold the body still.

113105.q: Which exercise is strength training with your own body weight?
113105.e: In a press-up, you push up your own body weight. For dumbbell curls, leg presses and bench presses, you need weights or machines.
113105.m: Press-ups are strength training with your own body weight.

113106.q: Why should teenagers first learn strength exercises with little weight?
113106.e: Poor technique can overload the joints and back. With a light weight, you first learn the movement correctly.
113106.m: In strength exercises, clean technique comes before heavy weight.

113107.q: What is the ability to coordinate the movements of the arms and legs, as in star jumps, called?
113107.e: Coupling ability links partial movements into one smooth sequence. You need it for a lay-up or star jumps, for example.
113107.m: Coupling ability coordinates the arms and legs.

113108.q: Which parts of the inner ear tell the brain about turns of the head?
113108.e: The semicircular canals of the balance organ are in the inner ear. They tell the brain about turns and the position of the head.
113108.m: The balance organ is in the inner ear.

113109.q: Which piece of equipment in the gym is particularly good for training balance?
113109.e: On the narrow balance beam, you constantly have to make small balancing movements. This trains balance.

113110.q: What is the ability to respond to a signal as quickly as possible, such as the starting gun, called?
113110.e: Reaction ability is one of the coordination abilities. Good goalkeepers and sprinters particularly need it.
113110.m: Anyone who responds quickly to signals has good reaction ability.

113111.q: Why is the age of about 7 to 12 a good time to learn new movements?
a: The muscles are at their biggest
The bones are at their hardest
113111.e: At this age, children learn new sequences of movement particularly quickly. This is often called the “golden age of learning”.
113111.m: Children of primary school age learn new movements particularly easily.

113112.q: Which exercise mainly trains hand-eye coordination?
113112.e: When juggling, the eyes must follow the balls and the hands must catch at exactly the right moment.
113112.m: Juggling trains the teamwork of eyes and hands.

113113.q: What is the ability to recognise a rhythm and turn it into movement, as in dancing, called?
113113.e: Rhythm ability is a coordination ability. You need it for dancing, skipping or hurdling.
113113.m: For dancing, you need good rhythm ability.

113114.q: What is the ability to sense your own position and movement in space, as in a somersault, called?
113114.e: In a somersault you need to know where up and down are. Orientation ability makes this possible.
113114.m: Orientation ability tells us our position in space.

113115.q: Apart from the muscles, what particularly determines how far a part of the body can move?
113115.e: Flexibility depends on the structure of the joints and on how far muscles, tendons and ligaments can stretch.
113115.m: Flexibility depends on joints and muscles.

113117.q: Which simple test measures the flexibility of the back and the backs of the thighs?
113117.e: In this test, you stretch your hands as far as possible towards your feet while sitting or standing. What is measured is how far you get.
113117.m: The sit and reach test shows how flexible the back and the backs of the legs are.

113118.q: What can happen if you only train strength and never practise flexibility?
113118.e: Anyone who only strengthens and never stretches or moves through the full range risks shortened muscles. This can affect posture.
113118.m: Strength and flexibility should be trained together.

113119.q: What is the gymnastic position called in which both legs are spread in a line flat on the floor?
113119.e: In the splits, both legs lie stretched out in a line on the floor. It is seen as a sign of great flexibility.
113119.m: For the splits, you need very flexible hips and legs.

113120.q: Which exercise shows how flexible the spine is backwards?
113120.e: In the bridge, you support yourself on your hands and feet and arch your back upwards. This needs a flexible spine.
113120.m: The bridge shows the flexibility of the spine.

113121.q: What do muscle cells absolutely need for aerobic energy production?
113121.e: “Aerobic” means “with oxygen”. The cells burn nutrients with oxygen to get energy.

113122.q: In which parts of the cell does aerobic energy production take place?
113122.e: The mitochondria are known as the “power stations of the cell”. Endurance training increases their number in muscle cells.
113122.m: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell.

113123.q: Which substances are produced as waste in aerobic energy production?
113123.e: Sugar and fat are broken down with oxygen. What is left is carbon dioxide, which we breathe out, and water.
113123.m: Aerobic energy production produces carbon dioxide and water.

113124.q: Which energy source is used more and more during long, easy exercise?
113124.e: Fat supplies a lot of energy, but can only be broken down with oxygen. During long, calm exercise, the body uses it more.
113124.m: During long, easy exercise, the body burns a lot of fat.

113125.q: During which kind of exercise does the body get its energy almost entirely aerobically?
113125.e: A marathon lasts hours, so the energy must be produced with oxygen. Short sprints and throws mainly run anaerobically.

113126.q: Where does the energy our muscles need for movement come from?
a: From the air we breathe out
113126.e: The muscles break down nutrients from food such as sugar and fat. This releases energy for movement.
113126.m: The energy for the muscles comes from food.

113127.q: Why do you breathe faster and more deeply during endurance sport?
113127.e: Working muscles need much more oxygen than at rest. Breathing faster and more deeply gets more oxygen into the blood.
113127.m: During exertion we breathe more to get more oxygen.

113128.q: What does a person’s maximum oxygen uptake show?
113128.e: Maximum oxygen uptake is the largest amount of oxygen the body can take in per minute. It is an important measure of endurance.
113128.m: Maximum oxygen uptake shows endurance performance.

113129.e: The prefix “an” means “without”. Anaerobically, the muscles get energy for a short time without using oxygen.

113130.q: What is the extra oxygen the body still takes in after very hard exercise, even though you are already resting, called?
113130.e: After a hard sprint, you keep breathing fast for a while. In this way the body makes up for the energy it produced earlier without enough oxygen.
113130.m: After hard exercise, the body pays back the oxygen debt.

113131.q: Roughly how long can you keep up a true flat-out sprinting speed?
113131.e: The muscles’ instant energy stores are largely empty after about 6 to 10 seconds of flat-out effort. After that you slow down.
113131.m: You can only hold full sprinting speed for a few seconds.

113132.q: In which event does anaerobic energy production play the biggest role?
113132.e: A 400-metre race is so intense that the oxygen is not enough. So the muscles get a large part of their energy without oxygen.
113132.m: Short, very hard races rely heavily on anaerobic energy.

113133.q: Why can you not keep up a sprinting pace for an hour?
113133.e: During very hard exercise, acidic waste products build up in the muscles. This forces you to slow down after a short time.
113133.m: At very high speed, the muscles quickly become too acidic.

113134.q: What do you feel when a lot of lactate builds up in the muscles during hard effort?
a: The muscles feel heavy and burn
113134.e: Lactate and acidic waste products build up during very hard exercise. The muscles then feel heavy and burn, and you have to slow down.
113134.m: A lot of lactate makes the muscles feel heavy and burn.

113135.q: Which energy source do the muscles use in anaerobic energy production with lactate formation?
113135.e: Only carbohydrates such as glucose can be broken down without oxygen. Fat always needs oxygen for this.
113135.m: Without oxygen, the muscles can only break down sugar.

113136.q: What helps to break down lactate faster after a hard run?
113136.e: During an easy cool-down jog, the lactate is used up with oxygen. This speeds up recovery.
113136.m: An easy cool-down jog helps break down lactate.

113137.q: Which simple rule of thumb is used to estimate maximum heart rate?
113137.e: The well-known rule of thumb is 220 minus age. It is only a rough estimate, because maximum heart rate varies from person to person.
113137.m: Maximum heart rate can be roughly estimated as 220 minus age.

113138.q: What maximum heart rate does the rule of thumb “220 minus age” give for a 14-year-old?
113138.e: 220 minus 14 equals 206 beats per minute. But the real value can differ considerably.
113138.m: For 14-year-olds, the rule of thumb gives 206 beats per minute.

113139.q: How does maximum heart rate change over the course of life?
113139.e: With increasing age, the heart can no longer beat as fast. That is why maximum heart rate decreases.
113139.m: Maximum heart rate decreases with age.

113140.q: How can you find your personal maximum heart rate more accurately than with a rule of thumb?
113140.e: In an exercise test, you increase the effort until you are exhausted while your pulse is measured. This should only be done if you are healthy and under supervision.
113140.m: An exercise test shows your personal maximum heart rate more accurately.

113141.q: Where on the body can you easily feel your own pulse?
113141.e: At the wrist on the thumb side, the radial artery lies just under the skin. You can feel the pulse well there, and also at the neck.
113141.m: You can feel your pulse well at the wrist or the neck.

113142.q: Roughly what percentage of maximum heart rate is easy basic endurance training done at?
113142.e: Basic endurance is trained at moderate effort, roughly 60 to 70 per cent of maximum heart rate. More than 100 per cent is not possible at all.
113142.m: Easy endurance training is at about two thirds of maximum heart rate.

113143.q: A person has a maximum heart rate of 200. Which pulse equals 70 per cent of that?
113143.e: 70 per cent of 200 is 0.7 times 200, so 140 beats per minute.
113143.m: Seventy per cent of 200 beats is 140 beats.

113144.q: Which device measures your pulse continuously during sport?
a: Heart rate watch with a sensor
113144.e: A heart rate watch measures the heart rate with a chest strap or a sensor on the wrist. That way you can see the effort straight away.
113144.m: With a heart rate watch you can monitor your effort during sport.

113145.q: What is the thickening of muscle fibres through strength training called?
113145.e: In hypertrophy, the individual muscle fibres become thicker. The opposite, muscle wasting, is called atrophy.
113145.m: Strength training makes muscle fibres thicker.

113146.q: Which nutrient is particularly important for building muscle?
113146.e: Muscles are made largely of protein. The body needs it to build new muscle after training.
113146.m: To build muscle, the body needs protein.

113147.q: When do muscles mainly grow after a training session?
113147.e: Training provides the stimulus, but the building happens during recovery. That is why breaks and sleep are important.
113147.m: Muscles grow during the recovery time after training.

113148.q: What is the principle called that the body recovers beyond its old level after a load?
113148.e: After training, the body does not just recover; it becomes a little more capable than before. This is called supercompensation.
113148.m: Through supercompensation, the body becomes stronger after training.

113149.q: What happens to muscles that are not used for weeks, for example because of a plaster cast?
113149.e: Unused muscles become thinner and weaker; this is called muscle wasting (atrophy). With training they can be built up again.

113150.q: Why is enough sleep important for building muscle?
113150.e: During sleep, the body releases growth hormones and repairs the muscles that have been worked. Too little sleep slows down muscle building.
113150.m: During sleep, the body recovers and repairs itself.

113151.q: Roughly how many skeletal muscles does a human have?
113151.e: Depending on how they are counted, humans have more than 600 skeletal muscles; the figure of around 650 is often given.
113151.m: Humans have more than 600 skeletal muscles.

113152.q: Which type of muscle do you move at will and build up through strength training?
a: Smooth muscle of the blood vessels
113152.e: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and can be controlled consciously. Heart muscle and smooth muscle work by themselves.
113152.m: Strength training builds up skeletal muscle.

113153.q: What is stretching called in which you hold a position calmly for several seconds?
113153.e: In static stretching, you hold the stretch without bouncing, for example for 20 to 30 seconds.
113153.m: In static stretching, you hold the position calmly.

113154.q: What is stretching with controlled swinging movements, such as leg swings, called?
113154.e: In dynamic stretching, you move deliberately into the stretch and out again. It is well suited to warming up.
113154.m: Dynamic stretching works with controlled movements.

113155.q: What should a correct stretch feel like?
a: A stabbing pain in the joint
113155.e: You only stretch until you feel a comfortable pull in the muscle. Pain is a warning signal that you have gone too far.
113155.m: Stretching should pull, but not hurt.

113156.q: Which muscle is stretched when you pull your heel towards your bottom while standing?
113156.e: Pulling the heel towards the bottom stretches the front of the thigh. That is where the four-headed thigh muscle, the quadriceps, is.
113156.m: Pulling the heel to the bottom stretches the front of the thigh.

113157.q: What should you do with your breathing when stretching?
a: Only force air out through the mouth
113157.e: Calm breathing helps the muscle relax. If you hold your breath, you tend to tense up.

113158.q: Which muscle is stretched when, in a lunge position, you keep your back heel on the floor and lean towards a wall?
113158.e: In this position, the back of the lower leg is stretched. That is where the calf muscle is.
113158.m: With your heel on the floor, you stretch the calf.

113159.q: Why should you not stretch with jerky bouncing?
a: It lowers the pulse too much
113159.e: Jerky bouncing triggers a protective reflex and can lead to small injuries in the muscle. It is better to stretch slowly and in a controlled way.

113160.q: Why do people stretch dynamically rather than holding long static stretches before a sprint?
a: Long holding can briefly reduce explosive strength
113160.e: Stretches held for a long time can make the muscles a little less explosive for a short while. That is why dynamic exercises are used before sprints and jumps.

113161.q: What is an injury from a blow or knock, which often causes a bruise, called?
113161.e: Contusions often happen in collisions, for example in football or ice hockey. Cooling and raising the injured part help against the swelling.
113161.m: A contusion is caused by a blow or knock.

113162.q: What is it called when a joint pops out of its normal position, for example in the shoulder?
113162.e: In a dislocation, the joint surfaces lose contact. The joint must be put back in place by a specialist.
113162.m: If a joint pops out of place, it is called a dislocation.

113163.q: Which ligament in the knee is particularly often torn in skiing and football injuries?
113163.e: The anterior cruciate ligament stabilises the knee during twisting movements. It often tears in falls with a twisted knee.
113163.m: The anterior cruciate ligament is a common injury in skiing and football.

113164.q: Which tendon connects the calf muscle to the heel bone?
113164.e: The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the body. It transfers the force of the calf to the heel.
113164.m: The Achilles tendon connects the calf and the heel.

113165.q: What helps most to prevent sports injuries?
113165.e: After warming up, body and mind are ready for the effort. This lowers the risk of strains and tears.

113166.q: What is the common injury called when you go over on the outside edge of your foot?
a: A ligament injury in the ankle
113166.e: When you go over on your ankle, the outer ligaments of the ankle joint are overstretched or torn. This is one of the most common sports injuries.
113166.m: Going over on your ankle often injures the ankle ligaments.

113167.q: What is overstretching of muscle fibres without a tear called?
113167.e: In a strain, muscle fibres are overstretched but not torn. If fibres tear, it is called a torn muscle fibre.
113167.m: A strain is an overstretching of the muscle.

113168.q: What is a broken bone called that is caused by many small overloads rather than an accident?
113168.e: If you run too much without enough recovery, the bone can get fine cracks. These can turn into a stress fracture, often in the foot.
113168.m: Too much load without a break can cause a stress fracture.

113169.q: What does the abbreviation J+S stand for in Swiss sport?
113169.e: Jugend+Sport (Youth+Sport) is the Confederation’s largest sports promotion programme for children and young people in Switzerland.

113170.q: Which federal office is responsible for Jugend+Sport?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
113170.e: Jugend+Sport is run by the Federal Office of Sport (FOSPO). It supports sports courses in clubs, schools and camps.
113170.m: The Federal Office of Sport runs Jugend+Sport.

113171.q: In which place in the canton of Bern is the Swiss Federal Institute of Sport?
113171.e: The institute is in Magglingen above Biel. The Federal Office of Sport also has its headquarters there.
113171.m: The Swiss Federal Institute of Sport is in Magglingen.

113172.q: Which age group is Jugend+Sport intended for?
113172.e: Jugend+Sport is aimed at children and young people aged 5 to 20. For the little ones, there is J+S children’s sport.
113172.m: Jugend+Sport is for children and young people aged 5 to 20.

113173.q: What is a person called who may lead sports courses after J+S training?
113173.e: Anyone who has attended a J+S leaders’ course becomes a J+S leader. After that, you must take further training regularly.
113173.m: J+S leaders run recognised sports courses.

113174.q: What is the aim of Jugend+Sport?
a: To get children and young people excited about sport
113174.e: Jugend+Sport supports sports courses and camps so that as many children and young people as possible enjoy doing sport regularly.
113174.m: Jugend+Sport wants to get children and young people excited about sport.

113175.q: Where in Ticino is the Confederation’s national youth sports centre?
113175.e: The Centro Sportivo Nazionale della Gioventù is in Tenero on Lake Maggiore. Many camps and courses take place there.
113175.m: The national youth sports centre is in Tenero.

113176.q: What do clubs receive from the Confederation when they run recognised J+S courses?
113176.e: The Confederation pays contributions for recognised J+S courses and camps. This allows clubs to offer cheap activities for children.
113176.m: For J+S courses, the Confederation pays clubs contributions.

113177.q: Why do endurance athletes often train in the mountains?
113177.e: At altitude the air pressure is lower, so you breathe in less oxygen with each breath. Over time, the body adapts to this lack.
113177.m: Altitude training uses the thin air in the mountains.

113178.q: Which blood cells does the body produce more of during altitude training?
113178.e: When oxygen is short, the body makes more of the cells that carry oxygen. This lets the blood bring more oxygen to the muscles.
113178.m: At altitude, the body makes more red blood cells.

113179.q: Which hormone stimulates the production of red blood cells and is banned as a doping substance when injected?
113179.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced naturally in the kidney. Given artificially, it is banned in sport.
113179.m: EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells.

113180.q: Which place in the Grisons at over 1,800 metres is known for altitude training?
113180.e: St Moritz is in the Upper Engadine at over 1,800 metres above sea level. Many runners and cross-country skiers train there at altitude.
113180.m: St Moritz is a well-known place for altitude training.

113181.q: What do you often notice during sport in the first few days at high altitude?
a: You get out of breath more quickly
113181.e: Because less oxygen arrives with each breath, you get tired more quickly with the same effort. After a few days, the body gets used to it.
113181.m: At high altitude, you get out of breath more quickly at first.

113182.q: What does the principle “live high, train low” describe?
a: Sleep high up, train lower down
Sleep lower down, train high up
113182.e: You live at altitude so that your blood adapts, but train lower down, where you can train harder.
113182.m: With “live high, train low”, you sleep high up and train lower down.

113183.q: What are health problems such as headaches and nausea when climbing too quickly to high altitudes called?
113183.e: If you climb too quickly to high altitudes, the body cannot adapt. Headaches and nausea are typical signs of altitude sickness.
113183.m: Climbing too quickly can cause altitude sickness.

113184.q: How long does an altitude training camp usually need to last at least to have an effect?
113184.e: The body needs time to make more red blood cells. Altitude training camps therefore often last two to four weeks.
113184.m: Altitude training needs several weeks to work.

113185.q: What is the endurance called that forms the basis for almost all sports and is built up with easy training?
113185.e: Basic endurance allows long efforts at medium intensity. It also helps you recover faster between hard sessions.
113185.m: Basic endurance is the foundation for many sports.

113186.q: What is the ability to adjust quickly to a new situation, for example when the ball bounces off unexpectedly, called?
113186.e: Adaptability lets you change a movement in a flash. It is particularly important in ball games.

113187.q: Why are the wrists particularly at risk when inline skating?
a: Because you often catch yourself with your hands when you fall
Because you move your hands while skating
Because the wheels rub against your hands
Because your hands sweat while skating
113187.e: When you fall, you stretch out your hands by reflex. Wrist guards prevent fractures and grazes when this happens.
113187.m: When inline skating, wrist guards protect against injuries.

113188.q: Why should you warm up your body briefly before stretching?
a: So that your pulse goes down
113188.e: Warmed-up muscles have a better blood supply and are more elastic. They can be stretched more easily and with less risk of injury.
113188.m: Warm muscles stretch better than cold ones.

113190.q: Which part of a DC motor reverses the current in the coil every half turn?
113190.e: The commutator reverses the direction of the current in the armature coil at exactly the right moment. So the motor keeps turning instead of stopping.
113190.m: The commutator keeps a DC motor turning.

113191.q: What does a magnetic field exert on a wire carrying a current?
113191.e: When current flows through a conductor in a magnetic field, a force acts on it, the Lorentz force. Every electric motor is based on this.
113191.m: In a magnetic field, a force acts on a current-carrying wire.

113192.q: How can you reverse the direction of rotation of a simple DC motor?
113192.e: If you reverse the voltage, the current flows the other way. This reverses the force in the magnetic field and the motor turns backwards.
113192.m: Reversing the connections of a DC motor changes its direction of rotation.

113193.q: Roughly how efficient are large electric motors?
113193.e: Large electric motors turn more than 90 per cent of the electrical energy into movement. Petrol engines manage much less.

113194.q: Which Swiss means of transport is driven by electric motors that draw current from the overhead line?
113194.e: The SBB (Swiss Federal Railways) runs almost entirely on electricity. The locomotives collect current from the overhead line via the pantograph.
113194.m: SBB trains are driven by electric motors.

113195.q: How do you increase the force of an electromagnet in a motor?
113195.e: More turns and more current produce a stronger magnetic field. An iron core strengthens it further.
113195.m: More turns make an electromagnet stronger.

113196.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a generator?
113196.e: In a generator a coil is turned in a magnetic field, or the other way round. This produces an electrical voltage.
113196.m: A generator turns movement into electric current.

113197.q: What drives the generator in a hydroelectric power station?
113197.e: The flowing water turns the turbine. This is connected to the generator and turns it too.
113197.m: In a hydroelectric power station, a turbine drives the generator.

113198.q: What happens to the voltage if you turn a generator faster?
113198.e: The faster the magnetic field in the coil changes, the higher the voltage produced.
113198.m: A generator turned faster gives more voltage.

113199.q: What is a wind turbine that produces electricity with a generator called?
113199.e: The wind turns the rotor blades, and these turn a generator. This produces electricity.
113199.m: A wind power plant uses a generator to make electricity from wind.

113200.q: Which power plant produces electricity without a turning generator?
113200.e: Solar cells turn light directly into electrical energy. All the other power plants named drive a generator.
113200.m: Solar cells produce electricity without a generator.

113201.q: Why does it get harder to turn a generator when many devices are connected?
113201.e: When more current flows, the coil's magnetic field brakes the rotation more strongly. You have to do more work because more energy is being supplied.
113201.m: The more current is drawn, the harder a generator is to turn.

113202.q: In which power stations does steam turn the turbine that drives the generator?
113202.e: In a nuclear power station, nuclear fission heats water into steam. The steam drives the turbine and so the generator.
113202.m: In nuclear power stations, steam drives the turbine.

113203.q: Which vehicle uses its electric motor as a generator when braking?
113203.e: When braking, the motor of an electric car becomes a generator and charges the battery. This is called regenerative braking.
113203.m: Electric cars recover electricity when braking.

113204.q: Which protective device in the fuse box uses induction to detect a fault current and switch off?
113204.e: The residual current device (RCD) compares the current flowing out and back in a small transformer. If some current flows away through a person, a voltage is induced and it switches off.
113204.m: An RCD protects against dangerous fault currents.

113205.q: What must change for a voltage to be induced in a coil?
a: The magnetic field in the coil
113205.e: Only a changing magnetic field produces an induced voltage. A stationary magnet in a stationary coil produces none.
113205.m: Induction needs a changing magnetic field.

113206.q: Which device uses induction to track down coins buried in the ground?
113206.e: A coil in the metal detector produces a changing magnetic field. If there is metal in the ground, it changes this field, and the device beeps.
113206.m: A metal detector finds metal using induction.

113207.q: What happens to the voltage if you pull a magnet out of a coil instead of pushing it in?
113207.e: When you push it in, the magnetic field increases; when you pull it out, it decreases. So the voltage points the other way.
113207.m: Reversing the movement reverses the voltage.

113208.q: How can you increase the induced voltage in a coil?
113208.e: More turns, a stronger magnet and faster movement increase the voltage. Slower movement lowers it.
113208.m: More turns give more induced voltage.

113209.q: Which kitchen appliance uses induction to heat the bottom of the pan directly?
113209.e: Under an induction hob a coil produces a changing magnetic field. It induces eddy currents in the bottom of the pan, which makes it hot.
113209.m: An induction hob heats the bottom of the pan directly.

113210.q: A copper pipe stands upright. What happens if you drop a strong magnet into it?
a: It falls much more slowly than usual
It sticks to the rim at the top
113210.e: The falling magnet induces currents in the copper pipe. These produce a magnetic field that brakes the magnet. So the induced current works against its cause.
113210.m: Induced currents brake the movement that creates them.

113211.q: How does the wireless charging of an electric toothbrush work?
113211.e: In the charging station a coil produces a changing magnetic field. It induces a voltage in a coil in the toothbrush.
113211.m: Wireless charging is based on induction.

113212.q: What is a dynamo on a bike for?
a: It produces electricity for the lights
113212.e: The dynamo is turned by the wheel and so produces electricity. This makes the front and rear lights shine.
113212.m: A bike dynamo produces electricity for the lights.

113213.q: What happens to a bike light without a battery when you stop at a red light?
113213.e: When the wheel stands still, the dynamo does not turn. Without movement no electricity is produced. That is why modern lights often have a standlight with storage.
113213.m: Without turning, a dynamo gives no electricity.

113214.q: Which German inventor developed the dynamo machine using the dynamo-electric principle in 1866?
113214.e: Werner von Siemens realised that the machine can strengthen its own magnetic field. This made large generators possible.
113214.m: Werner von Siemens invented the dynamo machine.

113215.q: Why do you have to pedal a bit harder when the bike dynamo is switched on?
a: The light makes the bike heavier
113215.e: The electrical energy for the light comes from the movement. You have to supply this extra energy with your legs.
113215.m: A dynamo turns pedal power into electricity.

113216.q: What type of current does a classic bike dynamo supply?
113216.e: In a dynamo a magnet turns past a coil. The direction of the voltage changes several times with each turn.
113216.m: A bike dynamo produces alternating current.

113217.q: What is the dynamo that runs against the side of the tyre called?
113217.e: With a bottle dynamo, a small wheel presses against the side of the tyre. In the wet it can slip.
113217.m: A bottle dynamo runs against the side of the tyre.

113218.q: Which emergency device produces its electricity with a small hand crank and a dynamo?
113218.e: With a wind-up torch you turn a crank that drives a small dynamo. So you don't need batteries.
113218.m: A wind-up torch produces electricity with a dynamo.

113219.q: What is the measuring device called that shows an alternating voltage as a curve on a screen?
113219.e: The oscilloscope plots how a voltage changes over time. This lets you see how the alternating voltage swings up and down.
113219.m: An oscilloscope makes the course of a voltage visible.

113220.q: Why can't you normally see a lamp on the 50-hertz mains flicker?
a: The eye is too slow for it
The current doesn't flow back and forth at all
The lamp stores light for hours
113220.e: The brightness changes too quickly for our eyes to notice each change. They see a steady light. In the Swiss power grid there are 50 cycles per second.
113220.m: For our eyes, flickering at 50 hertz is too fast.

113221.q: What is typical of alternating current?
a: The direction of the current keeps changing
It always flows in one direction
113221.e: With alternating current the direction changes regularly. With direct current it always flows the same way.

113222.q: At 50 hertz, how often does the current change direction in one second?
113222.e: One cycle has two changes of direction. At 50 cycles per second that makes 2 times 50, so 100 changes of direction.
113222.m: At 50 hertz the current changes direction 100 times a second.

113223.q: How many cycles per second does the alternating current from a socket in Switzerland have?
113223.e: The Swiss power grid has a frequency of 50 hertz. The voltage at the socket is 230 volts.

113224.q: Which inventor championed alternating current in the late 19th century?
113224.e: Nikola Tesla developed alternating current motors and systems. Thomas Edison, on the other hand, backed direct current; this is known as the war of the currents.

113225.q: How long does one complete cycle last at 50 hertz?
113225.e: The length of one cycle is 1 divided by 50: that makes 0.02 seconds.
113225.m: At 50 hertz one cycle lasts 0.02 seconds.

113226.q: What does the mains voltage look like on the screen of an oscilloscope?
113226.e: The mains voltage rises and falls evenly again and again. On the screen this makes a wavy line called a sine curve.
113226.m: Mains voltage runs like a wave.

113227.q: Which power source supplies direct current?
113227.e: A battery has a fixed positive and negative terminal. So the current always flows in the same direction.

113228.q: What kind of current do solar cells produce?
113228.e: Solar cells supply direct current because light always drives the charges in them in the same direction. For the household grid it still has to be converted.

113229.q: What is the device that converts direct current into alternating current called?
113229.e: An inverter turns direct current into alternating current, for example in solar installations. A rectifier does the opposite.
113229.m: An inverter turns direct current into alternating current.

113230.q: Which component lets current through in only one direction and is used for rectifying?
113230.e: A diode acts like a valve for current. With diodes you can turn alternating current into direct current.
113230.m: A diode lets current through in only one direction.

113231.q: Which inventor set up a direct current network in New York in the 1880s?
113231.e: In 1882 Thomas Edison opened a power station with a direct current network in New York. Later, however, alternating current won out.
113231.m: Thomas Edison built an early direct current network.

113232.q: What does a mobile phone charger plugged into the socket convert?
113232.e: A phone battery needs low-voltage direct current. The charger converts the alternating current from the socket accordingly.
113232.m: A charger turns alternating current into direct current.

113233.q: What voltage does an ordinary round AA battery have?
113233.e: An AA alkaline battery has a nominal voltage of 1.5 volts. For more voltage you connect several in series.

113234.q: What is the technology for sending electricity as direct current over very long distances called?
113234.e: With high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission there are fewer losses over very long distances. It is used, for example, for undersea cables.
113234.m: For very long distances, high-voltage direct current transmission is used.

113235.e: A transformer can raise or lower an alternating voltage. This is how the voltage is matched to power lines and devices.

113236.q: With which type of current does a transformer work?
113236.e: A transformer needs a changing magnetic field, so alternating current. With direct current no voltage is transferred.
113236.m: A transformer only works with alternating current.

113237.q: What does a transformer basically consist of?
a: Two coils on an iron core
A solar cell and a cable
113237.e: The primary coil and the secondary coil sit on a shared iron core. The core carries the magnetic field from one coil to the other.
113237.m: A transformer has two coils on an iron core.

113238.q: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary side and 2000 on the secondary side. What output voltage does it give with an input of 12 volts?
113238.e: The secondary coil has 2000 divided by 100, so 20 times more turns. The voltage therefore rises to 12 V times 20, which is 240 V.
113238.m: More turns on the secondary side raise the voltage.

113239.q: A coil with 200 turns is connected to 10 volts. How many turns does the secondary coil need for 40 volts?
113239.e: The voltage is to become four times bigger, so four times more turns are needed: 200 times 4 makes 800.
113239.m: Four times the voltage needs four times the number of turns.

113240.q: What is the coil of a transformer called to which the input voltage is applied?
113240.e: The input voltage is applied to the primary coil. The converted voltage is taken from the secondary coil.
113240.m: The input voltage is applied to the primary coil.

113241.q: Why does a large transformer get warm when it is running?
113241.e: In the wire and the iron core a small part of the energy is lost as heat. Large transformers are therefore cooled with oil or air.
113241.m: Losses in a transformer turn into heat.

113242.q: Where in a neighbourhood are the transformers that lower the voltage for homes to 230 and 400 volts?
113242.e: Transformer substations lower the medium voltage of the distribution grid to the low voltage used in homes. You see them as small huts in neighbourhoods.
113242.m: Transformer substations bring the voltage down to household level.

113243.q: Why is electricity transported over long distances at very high voltage?
a: So that less energy is lost
So that the cables are lighter
So that the current flows faster
So that there is less lightning
113243.e: At high voltage less current is needed for the same power. Less current means less heat loss in the lines.
113243.m: High voltage reduces losses when transporting electricity.

113244.q: What is the highest voltage in the Swiss transmission grid?
113244.e: The highest voltage level in Switzerland is 380 kilovolts, which is 380,000 volts. There are also lines with 220 kilovolts.
113244.m: The Swiss extra-high-voltage grid runs at 380 kilovolts.

113245.q: Which company operates the Swiss extra-high-voltage transmission grid?
113245.e: Swissgrid is the national grid company. It operates and monitors Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid.
113245.m: Swissgrid operates the Swiss extra-high-voltage grid.

113246.q: Why can a bird sit safely on a single high-voltage line?
a: Its feathers are made of rubber
113246.e: Both feet are on the same wire, so there is almost no voltage difference. It only becomes dangerous if it touches the ground or a second wire at the same time.
113246.m: Without a voltage difference, no current flows through the body.

113247.q: Why must you never fly kites under high-voltage lines?
a: There is a risk of electric shock
The wind is too weak there
113247.e: A kite string can conduct electricity, especially when damp. If it comes close to the line, a deadly electric arc can form.
113247.m: Never fly kites under high-voltage lines.

113248.q: What are the tall steel structures that high-voltage lines hang from called?
113248.e: Pylons hold the conductor cables high above the ground. This keeps a safe distance from people, buildings and trees.

113249.q: What are the insulators on a pylon for?
a: They separate the line and the pylon electrically
113249.e: Insulators made of glass, porcelain or plastic do not conduct electricity. They stop the current flowing through the pylon into the ground.
113249.m: Insulators stop current flowing into the pylon.

113250.q: Instead of on pylons, where are high-voltage lines sometimes laid?
113250.e: Underground cables are invisible in the landscape, but more expensive and complicated. In Switzerland they are used, for example, in sensitive landscapes.
113250.m: High voltage can also flow through underground cables.

113251.q: Roughly what share of Swiss electricity production came from hydropower in 2024?
113251.e: Hydropower is Switzerland's most important source of electricity. In 2024, according to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, it supplied around 60 per cent of the country's production.
113251.m: Hydropower supplies more than half of Swiss electricity.

113252.q: Which form of the water's energy does a hydroelectric power station use?
113252.e: Water high up has potential energy. As it flows down, this becomes kinetic energy, which turns the turbine.
113252.m: Hydroelectric power stations use the potential and kinetic energy of water.

113253.q: Why does water from a high reservoir in the Alps provide especially much energy?
a: It falls a long way and becomes fast
It is colder than river water
It is cleaner than river water
113253.e: The greater the height of the fall, the more potential energy the water has. At the bottom it hits the turbine at high speed.
113253.m: A big drop means a lot of energy.

113254.q: What is typical of a river power station, for example on the Rhine?
a: A small drop, but a great deal of water
A big drop, but little water
It needs no water at all
It only uses rainwater from the roof
113254.e: A river power station only dams the river by a few metres. In return, a great deal of water flows through the turbines every second.
113254.m: River power stations use lots of water with a small drop.

113255.q: What is an advantage of hydropower over coal-fired power stations?
113255.e: No fuel is burnt when a hydroelectric power station is running. So hardly any carbon dioxide is produced.
113255.m: Hydropower is renewable energy with little CO2.

113256.q: What are the steps for fish called that help them swim past a river power station?
113256.e: A fish ladder is made of small pools with a gentle slope. This lets fish get round the power station going upstream.
113256.m: Fish ladders help fish get past power stations.

113257.q: Which device at the water intake keeps driftwood and leaves away from the turbines?
113257.e: A rack of steel bars catches branches, leaves and rubbish. A cleaning machine removes the material regularly.
113257.m: A trash rack protects the turbines from floating debris.

113258.q: Which factors does the output of a hydroelectric power station mainly depend on?
a: Amount of water and height of the drop
Taste and depth of the water
Fish population and length of the bank
113258.e: The more water per second and the bigger the drop, the more power a station can produce.
113258.m: The output depends on the amount of water and the drop.

113259.q: What does a run-of-river power station use?
a: The water of a mountain lake
113259.e: A run-of-river power station stands right on a river and uses its continuously flowing water. It only dams the river a little.
113259.m: Run-of-river power stations use the water of rivers.

113260.q: What is the drop typically like at a run-of-river power station?
113260.e: Run-of-river power stations usually dam the river by only a few metres. They make up for the small drop with lots of water.
113260.m: Run-of-river power stations have a small drop.

113261.q: When do run-of-river power stations in Switzerland produce the most electricity?
a: In summer, when the snow melts
Only when there is no wind
113261.e: In early summer and summer, rivers carry a lot of water because of melting snow. In winter there is less water.
113261.m: Run-of-river power stations produce a lot of electricity in summer.

113262.q: On which large river on the border with Germany are there several Swiss run-of-river power stations?
113262.e: On the High Rhine between Lake Constance and Basel there are numerous run-of-river power stations, for example at Rheinfelden and Laufenburg.
113262.m: There are many run-of-river power stations on the High Rhine.

113263.q: What is typical of the electricity production of a run-of-river power station?
a: It only runs during the day
113263.e: The river flows all the time, so run-of-river power stations produce constantly. This is called baseload energy.
113263.m: Run-of-river power stations supply electricity constantly.

113264.q: What is the structure called with which a run-of-river power station dams the river a little?
113264.e: A weir dams the river by a few metres. This creates the drop that the power station uses.
113264.m: A weir dams the river for the power station.

113265.q: Why can a run-of-river power station hardly shift its production to other times?
113265.e: The water flows straight through and is hardly stored. So the station produces when the water comes, not when it is needed.
113265.m: Run-of-river power stations can hardly store water.

113266.q: What is the part of a river power station called in which the turbines and generators stand?
113266.e: The turbines and generators are housed in the powerhouse. It is often right next to the weir in the river.
113266.m: Turbines and generators stand in the powerhouse.

113267.q: What is the big advantage of a storage power station?
113267.e: The water is collected in a reservoir. It can then be released when a lot of electricity is needed, for example in winter.
113267.m: Storage power stations supply electricity when it is needed.

113268.q: What is the water called that must stay in a stream below a water intake so that animals and plants survive?
113268.e: The Water Protection Act requires that not all the water is diverted for producing electricity. The required amount is called the residual flow.
113268.m: Residual flow protects life in the stream below an intake.

113269.q: What is the minimum number of water basins a pumped storage power station needs?
113269.e: It needs an upper and a lower basin. Between them, water is pumped up or let down as needed.
113269.m: A pumped storage power station needs an upper and a lower basin.

113270.q: Why are pumped storage power stations built mainly in the mountains?
a: Because there are big height differences between two basins there
Because less electricity is needed there
Because the Sun shines more strongly there
Because water is lighter in the mountains
113270.e: The higher the upper basin is above the lower one, the more energy there is in the water. In the Alps such height differences are found over short distances.
113270.m: Pumped storage power stations need a big height difference.

113271.q: Why is a pumped storage power station not really an energy producer?
a: It uses more electricity than it supplies
113271.e: There are losses when pumping water up and letting it flow back. So the station is above all a giant battery.
113271.m: A pumped storage power station works like a giant battery.

113272.q: What is the place in the mountains called where water is collected for a storage power station?
113272.e: A dam holds the water back in a reservoir. From there it flows through penstocks to the power station.
113272.m: Storage power stations collect water in reservoirs.

113273.q: How does the water get from the reservoir down to the turbines?
113273.e: Penstocks carry the water steeply downhill. At the bottom the water pressure is very high and drives the turbines powerfully.
113273.m: Penstocks bring the water to the turbines.

113274.q: When do the reservoirs in the Alps fill up the most?
113274.e: In summer snow and glaciers melt and the lakes fill up. In winter the water is used when more electricity is needed.
113274.m: Alpine reservoirs fill up in summer.

113276.q: What rises from the large cooling tower of the Gösgen nuclear power station?
113276.e: In the cooling tower, cooling water is cooled by air. Some of it evaporates, and the visible cloud is water vapour, not smoke.
113276.m: Water vapour rises from the cooling tower.

113277.q: What drives the generator that produces electricity at the Gösgen nuclear power station?
113277.e: The heat from the reactor turns water into steam. The steam turns a turbine, and this drives the generator.
113277.m: In a nuclear power station, steam drives a turbine.

113278.q: Which fuel is split in the Gösgen nuclear power station?
113278.e: The fuel rods contain uranium nuclei. When they split, a lot of heat is released, which heats water into steam.
113278.m: In a nuclear power station, uranium nuclei are split.

113279.q: Which Swiss nuclear power station has a greater output than Gösgen?
113279.e: Leibstadt in Aargau is the most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland, with Gösgen in second place.
113279.m: Leibstadt is Switzerland's most powerful nuclear power station.

113280.q: Roughly what share of Swiss electricity do nuclear power stations such as Gösgen supply together?
113280.e: Together the Swiss nuclear power stations supply about a third of the electricity. Hydropower supplies the largest share.
113280.m: Nuclear power stations supply around a third of Swiss electricity.

113281.q: Why is the Gösgen nuclear power station shut down for a few weeks every year?
a: For maintenance and changing fuel rods
Because nobody needs electricity in summer
So that the Aare becomes clean again
Because the uranium would otherwise freeze
113281.e: During the yearly overhaul, used fuel rods are replaced and parts of the plant are checked. A supervisory authority checks safety at the same time.
113281.m: Nuclear power stations are regularly maintained and inspected.

113282.q: How do traffic lights often detect that a car is waiting in front of them?
a: With an induction loop in the road
With a microphone on the post
With scales under the road surface
113282.e: In the road surface there is a wire loop with an alternating field. The metal of the car changes this field, and the system registers the vehicle.
113282.m: Induction loops in the road detect waiting cars.

113283.q: A transformer lowers 230 volts to 23 volts. What is the ratio of turns of the primary coil to the secondary coil?
113283.e: The voltage falls to a tenth, because 230 divided by 23 makes 10. So the primary coil has ten times as many turns as the secondary coil.
113283.m: A tenth of the voltage needs a tenth of the turns.

113284.q: What is the three-phase alternating current called that cookers and large machines run on?
113284.e: Three-phase current consists of three alternating currents that are offset from each other. It is ideal for powerful motors and large appliances.
113284.m: Three-phase current consists of three alternating currents.

113285.q: Why does a glacier move down the valley?
113285.e: The heavy ice slowly changes shape under its own weight and flows downhill, following gravity.
113285.m: A glacier flows slowly down the valley because of gravity.

113286.q: Where does the ice of a valley glacier flow fastest at the surface?
113286.e: At the edges and the bottom, friction with the rock slows the ice down. In the middle, the friction is smallest, so the ice flows fastest there.
113286.m: A glacier flows faster in the middle than at the edge.

113287.q: What are the deep cracks in glacier ice called?
113287.e: Where the ice moves at different speeds or flows over a steep step, the brittle surface ice tears open. This creates crevasses.
113287.m: Crevasses form when the ice tears apart as it flows.

113288.q: What helps a glacier slide over the rock underneath?
113288.e: Meltwater on the underside of the glacier works like a lubricant. The ice then slides more easily over the rock.
113288.m: Water under the ice makes glaciers slide.

113289.q: What happens to the ice when a glacier flows over a steep rock step?
a: It breaks up into many crevasses and blocks
113289.e: At steep steps, the ice tears open and forms towers and blocks. This area is called an icefall.
113289.m: At steep steps, a glacier breaks up.

113290.q: What marks does a glacier leave on rock that it has polished smooth?
113290.e: Stones frozen into the ice at the bottom of the glacier scratch grooves into the rock as it flows. These grooves are called glacial striations.
113290.m: Glacial striations show which way a glacier flowed.

113291.q: What shape of valley do big glaciers typically leave behind?
113291.e: A glacier scrapes out the floor and sides of a valley, making it wide. This creates a U-shaped trough, while rivers tend to cut V-shaped valleys.
113291.m: Glaciers shape valleys into a U, rivers into a V.

113292.q: Roughly how fast do most Alpine glaciers move?
a: A few metres to a few hundred metres a year
113292.e: Alpine glaciers usually flow only a few centimetres to just under a metre a day. That adds up to a few metres to a few hundred metres a year.
113292.m: Glaciers move so slowly that you can hardly see it with the naked eye.

113293.q: Which type of glacier fills a hollow below a mountain peak and does not form a long tongue?
113293.e: A cirque glacier lies in a hollow, the cirque, below a ridge. It is small and does not reach far down into the valley.
113293.m: A cirque glacier lies in a hollow and has no long tongue.

113294.q: From which high railway destination, with the “Top of Europe” station, can you look down on the start of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
113294.e: The Jungfrau Railway goes up to the Jungfraujoch at about 3450 metres. From there you can see the Jungfraufirn, which flows into the Aletsch Glacier.
113294.m: From the Jungfraujoch, you can see where the Aletsch Glacier gathers its ice.

113295.q: Why does the Great Aletsch Glacier get shorter every year?
a: Because it is getting warmer and more ice is melting
Because too much snow falls in winter
113295.e: Because of global warming, more ice melts in summer than new ice is added in winter. That is why the glacier is retreating.
113295.m: The Aletsch Glacier is shrinking because of warming.

113296.q: What is special about the Great Aletsch Glacier?
a: It is the largest glacier in the Alps
It is the only glacier in Switzerland
113296.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the longest and largest glacier in the Alps.
113296.m: The Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.

113297.q: Roughly how long is the Great Aletsch Glacier today?
113297.e: From the snowfields at the Jungfrau to its tongue, the glacier measures about 20 to 23 kilometres, depending on the measurement. But it gets shorter every year.
113297.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier is a good 20 kilometres long.

113298.q: In which canton is most of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
113298.e: The glacier starts at the Jungfrau and flows through Valais towards the Rhône valley.
113298.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier is in Valais.

113299.q: Which big river does the meltwater from the Great Aletsch Glacier flow into?
113299.e: The meltwater flows through a gorge down into the Rhône valley and joins the Rhône near Brig.
113299.m: The water of the Aletsch Glacier flows into the Rhône.

113300.q: Which conifer grows in the Aletsch Forest and can live for several hundred years there?
113300.e: The Aletsch Forest lies above the glacier and is a nature reserve. Some Swiss stone pines there are several hundred years old.
113300.m: Ancient Swiss stone pines grow in the Aletsch Forest.

113301.q: What are the dark stripes called that run lengthways along the Great Aletsch Glacier?
113301.e: Where two streams of ice flow together, their side moraines join to form a band of rubble on the ice. On the Aletsch Glacier you can see these medial moraines as dark stripes.
113301.m: Medial moraines form where two glaciers flow together.

113302.q: At the edge of the Aletsch Glacier, the ice dams up a lake. What can happen if a lake like this suddenly drains?
113302.e: If the ice breaks, all the water flows out at once. In the past, this caused dangerous floods at the Aletsch Glacier.
113302.m: Glacier lakes can suddenly drain and cause floods.

113303.q: What is the main cause of glaciers shrinking in the Alps today?
113303.e: Because of human-made global warming, more ice melts in summer than is replaced by snow in winter. That is why the glaciers are getting smaller.
113303.m: Glaciers are melting because of global warming.

113304.q: According to GLAMOS, what percentage of their ice volume did Swiss glaciers lose in the record year 2022?
113304.e: Because of little winter snow, Sahara dust and a hot summer, Swiss glaciers lost about 6 per cent of their volume in 2022. That was the biggest loss ever measured.
113304.m: In 2022, Swiss glaciers melted more than ever measured before.

113305.q: Why does dark dust or rubble on the ice speed up melting?
a: Dark surfaces absorb more heat from the sun
Dust contains salt that dissolves ice
113305.e: Light surfaces reflect a lot of sunlight, while dark ones absorb more energy. This reflecting power is called albedo.
113305.m: Dark ice melts faster because it absorbs more sunlight.

113306.q: What unusual measure is used to protect part of the ice of the Rhône Glacier in summer?
113306.e: Near the Hotel Belvédère on the Furka Pass, the ice grotto in the Rhône Glacier is covered with light fleece blankets. They reflect sunlight and slow down the melting in that spot.
113306.m: Light blankets can slow down melting in small areas.

113307.q: For which Swiss glacier was a symbolic funeral held in 2019 because it had almost disappeared?
113307.e: The small Pizol Glacier in the canton of St Gallen had shrunk so much that it was removed from the measuring network. In 2019, a farewell ceremony was held for it.
113307.m: The Pizol Glacier was symbolically said goodbye to in 2019.

113308.q: What is ice called that has broken away from a shrinking glacier and no longer flows?
113308.e: When a glacier becomes very thin, the supply of ice from above is cut off. The leftover chunks of ice no longer move and are called dead ice.
113308.m: Dead ice is glacier ice that no longer flows.

113309.q: How does the path to the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine show the glacier's retreat?
a: With signs that mark earlier glacier positions with the year
With a clock that measures the melting
With a lift that is made longer every year
With flags on the glacier ice
113309.e: Along the path there are signs with years showing where the tongue of the glacier used to end. So you walk through the history of its retreat.
113309.m: At the Morteratsch Glacier, signs show how far the glacier used to reach.

113310.q: What happened in the Lötschental in May 2025 after the Birch Glacier collapsed?
a: Most of the village of Blatten was buried
The glacier grew by a kilometre
113310.e: Huge amounts of rock and ice from the Birch Glacier crashed into the valley and buried most of Blatten. The village had been evacuated beforehand because of the danger.
113310.m: The collapse of the Birch Glacier buried the village of Blatten in 2025.

113311.q: According to GLAMOS, what percentage of their ice volume did Swiss glaciers lose in 2026?
113311.e: After a winter with little snow and a hot summer, Swiss glaciers lost more than 5 per cent of their volume in 2026. That was just a little less than in the record year 2022.
